title: The Call and Its Testing
subtitle: How to discern a call to ministry without presumption and without false humility, what Scripture requires, how the church confirms, and how to wait well.
pillar: The Arc of a Leadership Life

parts.title: The Real Question
parts.body:
There is a sentence you have been carrying, maybe for years: I think I might be called to ministry. You have said it out loud to almost no one, because both possible answers frighten you. If it is true, your life changes shape. If it is false, you have been flattering yourself in the most spiritual vocabulary available.

Two ditches run alongside this road. The first is presumption: the man who anoints himself, who hears his own ambition and calls it the voice of God, who needs the title more than the work. The second is false humility: the man who feels the weight of a true call and keeps deferring it, telling himself he is unworthy, when what he actually fears is the cost. Both ditches are full of people. I have stood at the edge of both. And the presumptuous man and the falsely humble man have one thing in common: each made his decision alone.

The desire itself does not settle the question, but neither does it disqualify you. Paul calls the aspiration noble before he says a single word about fitness. So the real question is not whether you want this. Wanting it is allowed. The real question is whether you will let the desire be tested by something other than itself: by Scripture's plain qualifications, by the people who know your actual life, by the church that alone can lay hands on you, and by time. A call that cannot survive testing was not a call. A call that refuses testing is already disqualified.

parts.title: Why It Matters
parts.body:
Get this wrong in the first direction and you get the self-appointed shepherd: the man in the pulpit because he needed an audience, the planter whose church exists to solve his identity problem, the leader who confused giftedness with calling and charisma with character. The people under him become props in his discernment process, except the process ended years ago and they were never consulted. Most of the wreckage this hub catalogs began at this exact fork, with a desire nobody tested.

Get it wrong in the other direction and the loss is quieter but real. Somewhere there is a congregation that needed the shepherd who talked himself out of it. The man who mistook his fear for humility, his comfort for contentment, his timidity for prudence. False humility looks like virtue and functions like disobedience. Moses tried it at the bush, and the text says the anger of the Lord was kindled against him, which should unsettle anyone hiding behind I am not able.

And the question matters for the watching congregation, because how a church discerns its leaders teaches the whole body what ministry is. A church that ordains charisma will harvest collapse. A church that tests slowly, prays honestly, and confirms publicly is teaching every member that the work belongs to God before it belongs to anyone's resume. The stakes are not only the candidate's soul. They are the next thirty years of some congregation's life. Discernment is not a private hobby. It is an act of love toward people you have not met.

parts.title: The Biblical Foundation
parts.body:
Paul opens the qualification text with a blessing on the desire. The saying is trustworthy: if anyone aspires to the office of overseer, he desires a noble task. First Timothy 3:1 stands against every tradition of pious throat-clearing that treats wanting the work as evidence of unfitness for it. The aspiration is called noble before a single qualification is named. God does not despise the longing he plants.

But notice what the qualifications actually are. Read 1 Timothy 3:2 to 7 and Titus 1:6 to 9 slowly and the list is almost disappointingly ordinary: sober-minded, self-controlled, hospitable, not a drunkard, not violent, not quarrelsome, not a lover of money, a good manager of his own household, well thought of by outsiders. One gift appears, able to teach. Everything else is character any mature Christian should possess. The list is not a job posting. It is a mirror. It asks not, are you talented, but, are you the kind of man whose ordinary life will survive being watched.

Then Scripture closes the door on self-appointment. Hebrews 5:4: no one takes this honor for himself, but only when called by God, just as Aaron was. Even Christ, the writer continues, did not exalt himself to be made high priest. If the Son did not appoint himself, the matter is settled for the rest of us. Jeremiah 23:21 gives the negative print: I did not send the prophets, yet they ran. Running is easy. Being sent is the question.

And the sending is verified in public. In Acts 13 the call to Barnabas and Saul comes while the church at Antioch is worshiping and fasting, and the church fasts again, prays, lays on hands, and sends them off. Timothy was already well spoken of by the brothers at Lystra and Iconium before Paul took him along, and his gift came through prophecy when the council of elders laid hands on him. The pattern never shows a man alone in a room concluding he is called and informing the church afterward. Desire rises in the individual. Confirmation belongs to the church. There are no self-appointed shepherds in the New Testament, only wolves who appointed themselves.

And between desire and confirmation, Scripture builds in years. David is anointed in 1 Samuel 16 and crowned decades later, with caves in between. Moses gets forty years of sheep. Paul, blinded on the road, still spends years in Arabia and Tarsus before Barnabas comes looking for him. The waiting is not bureaucratic delay. It is part of the call.

parts.title: The Historical Witness
parts.body:
The men the church remembers best are the ones who ran. Gregory of Nazianzus, ordained by his own father around Christmas of 361, fled to Pontus within weeks and had to write one of the great documents of pastoral theology, his second oration, to explain himself: he had not despised the office, he had measured it. Augustine wept through his ordination at Hippo in 391, seized by a congregation that had effectively kidnapped its candidate while he was praying for someone else to be chosen. John Chrysostom built On the Priesthood around the story of his own evasion, arguing that his flight honored the office more than eager acceptance would have, because he had seen what the work weighs.

Their reluctance was not a performance. It was the testing working as designed. The early church assumed that the man who grasped at the office thereby revealed his unfitness for it, and the centuries that followed proved the assumption every time they ignored it, most lavishly in the simony of the medieval church, where calls were purchased like fields and the purchasers shepherded accordingly.

The Reformers gave the testing its grammar. Calvin distinguished the secret call, that honest testimony of the heart known to God alone, from the external call, the church's public judgment and ordering, and insisted both were necessary. His own story enacts the doctrine: he wanted a scholar's quiet life, and in 1536 Guillaume Farel threatened him with God's curse on his studies if he abandoned Geneva. Calvin stayed. The call came to him in another man's voice, which is roughly how it usually comes.

Spurgeon's word to his students belongs here, weighed fairly. If you can do anything else, do it, he said in substance, and the line has been both abused and misread. He did not mean that any detectable ability disqualifies you. He meant that the man who can be content outside the ministry should stay outside it, because contentment elsewhere is evidence, and the work is too heavy for the half-hearted. But Spurgeon never made the burning desire sufficient on its own. He required aptness to teach, fruit in actual hearers, and the sober judgment of the church alongside it. The desire opens the inquiry. It does not close it.

parts.title: The Traditions and the Debates
parts.body: This is a wisdom topic, not a contested command. Scripture requires that shepherds be called, qualified, and confirmed, and no tradition disputes it. The live debate is about how the call ordinarily arrives, and two great traditions have answered differently. Both are older than the people currently arguing about them. Both are holding something true.

views.name: The crisis-call tradition
views.body: In this tradition the call is an event: datable, often dramatic, sometimes resisted, finally undeniable. Its precedents are weighty. Isaiah sees the throne and the smoke. Jeremiah is told he was appointed before he was formed. Paul is knocked into the dirt on the Damascus road. The revival traditions, the Baptists and Methodists and Pentecostals who carried the gospel to the frontier and the global south, were built by men and women who could tell you the night God called them. The strength of this view is what it does in the dark. The pastor who has stood in the fire of an unmistakable commission does not resign when the committee turns hostile or the plant stalls, because he answers to a memory stronger than his circumstances. A call you can date is a call you can return to.

views.name: The providence-and-gifting tradition
views.body: In this tradition the call ordinarily arrives without thunder: through gifts the church notices, doors providence opens, character that holds under inspection, and a congregation's sober judgment. Its advocates point out that 1 Timothy 3 lists no required experience, only observable character and one teaching gift, and that Timothy himself appears to be called through family faith, public reputation, and the elders' hands rather than through any recorded crisis. The strength of this view is its protection against counterfeits. Feelings can be manufactured, and the man most certain of his dramatic call is sometimes the man most resistant to testing. A call resting on confirmed gifting and the church's public act does not evaporate when the emotions do, because it was never founded on them. God's ordinary way is means, not lightning, and means leave a paper trail the church can read.

parts.title: The Scholarship, Christian and Secular
parts.body: The Christian shelf on calling is long and surprisingly unsentimental. The secular shelf knows real things about gifting, fit, and perseverance, and every one of them must still answer to a Lord who calls men away from their strengths as often as into them.

christian.author: C. H. Spurgeon
christian.note: The chapter on the call to the ministry is the source of the famous test and its necessary context. Spurgeon demands an intense, all-absorbing desire, aptness to teach, some measure of fruit among actual hearers, and the judgment of the church. Four tests, not one. Quoting only the first is how the line gets abused.

christian.author: Edmund Clowney
christian.note: Clowney grounds calling in the call of the gospel itself: every believer is called to Christ before anyone is called to an office. His ordering keeps the office from swallowing the man, and his treatment of gifts discerned in the body remains the clearest short account of external confirmation in print.

christian.author: Os Guinness
christian.note: Guinness distinguishes the primary call, to Someone, from secondary calls, to something, and shows what happens when traditions confuse them: the medieval error that spiritualized clergy above everyone else, and the modern error that flattens calling into career. Useful precisely because it refuses to make ministry the only calling that counts.

christian.author: Charles Bridges
christian.note: The 1830 classic that a century of pastors carried into the work. Bridges examines the inquiry into one's call with surgical patience, including the section every candidate should read twice, on corrupt motives that wear clerical dress: love of distinction, love of literature, family expectation, the desire for a respectable post.

secular.source: So Good They Can't Ignore You
secular.author: Cal Newport
secular.whatItGetsRight: Newport dismantles the follow-your-passion script with case studies showing that passion usually follows competence rather than preceding it. People come to love work they have become good at, through deliberate practice and what he calls career capital. Applied to ministry, it is a fair warning against ordaining a feeling before any evidence of fruit exists.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Newport's frame is acquisition: build rare skills, then trade them for autonomy and mission. The call of God is not a trade and cannot be earned into existence. Moses is sent with a slow tongue and Paul's thorn stays in, because sometimes God calls directly through weakness so the power is plainly his. Competence matters, the church must see aptness to teach, but the call comes down from God. It does not come up from a skill stack.

secular.author: Marcus Buckingham and Donald Clifton
secular.whatItGetsRight: The strengths research gave ordinary people a vocabulary for what the church calls gifting: stable patterns of talent that are observable, nameable, and most fruitful when developed rather than ignored. Elder boards discerning a candidate are doing informally what this research does with instruments, and the instruments occasionally see what flattery hides.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: An inventory can describe the vessel. It cannot issue the commission. Scripture's qualification lists are dominated by character, not talent themes, and the Spirit distributes gifts as he wills, for the common good, not for self-actualization. A strengths profile that becomes the final word on calling has replaced the church's discernment with a questionnaire, and replaced the Caller with the wiring.

secular.author: Angela Duckworth
secular.whatItGetsRight: Duckworth's research found that sustained passion joined to perseverance predicts achievement better than raw talent does. Ministry is a long obedience, and her finding that people quit good work mostly in the middle, not at the beginning, matches every pastor's tenth year. The call will need to outlast the feelings that accompanied it.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Grit locates the staying power in the self, and the self runs out. The biblical word is not grit but faithfulness, and its engine is outside the man: he who calls you is faithful, he will surely do it. Perseverance in ministry is not a personality trait successfully deployed. It is a daily gift received, which is why exhausted pastors need grace and rest, not exhortations to be grittier.

parts.title: The Formation
parts.body:
The testing of a call is not an obstacle course God watches from a distance. It is the first stage of the formation the call requires, and skipping it produces exactly the leaders this hub keeps lamenting.

Waiting is the first work, and waiting well is a skill almost no one arrives with. The years between desire and confirmation feel like denial. They are usually preparation. David learned the shepherd's patience on actual sheep and the king's restraint in actual caves, and the man who reached the throne without those years would have been Saul with better press. If you are in the waiting now, the question is not how to shorten it. The question is what it is for. Somewhere in the delay is a specific lesson with your name on it, and the delay ends when the lesson does, on a schedule you do not control.

Obscurity is the second work. Before God gives a man a platform he generally gives him a hiddenness, and what you do there is the truest data about your call that exists. Teach the class of four. Visit the man nobody visits. If the work only interests you with an audience attached, that is not a call to ministry. It is a call to attention, and it should be starved, not staffed.

The third work is the purifying of the desire itself. The aspiration Paul blesses rarely starts pure in anyone. Mixed in with the love of Christ and his church are the love of mattering, the hunger of old wounds, the father you are still trying to impress. I came into ministry carrying all of that, and some of it I only saw years in. God is not waiting for the desire to be sterile before he uses you. He is asking whether you will let him keep refining it after the title arrives, which is when the refining usually stops.

parts.title: The Practice
parts.body: Discernment is not a mood. It is a set of actions taken in company, over time, with witnesses. Start where you are.

steps: Say the sentence out loud this month to one wise believer who knows your actual life. Secret discernment is not discernment.
Read 1 Timothy 3:1 to 7 and Titus 1:6 to 9 with your spouse or closest friend and ask them to measure you honestly against each line. Listen without defending yourself.
Begin serving now in a role with no title and no stage, and pay attention to whether the work itself, without the office, still draws you.
Ask your elders to test you formally: a teaching opportunity they evaluate, a season of service they observe, a scheduled conversation where they tell you the truth.
Treat delay and closed doors as data from a good Father, not as a verdict on your worth. Write down what each season is teaching you, because you will forget.
Name your motives on paper, including the embarrassing ones, and show the paper to a mentor. The mixed motive you confess loses power. The one you hide compounds.
Keep a record of your confirmation: who affirmed the call, what they saw, the day hands were laid on you. There will be a Tuesday in year six when you need the file.
Stay under real authority from the first day. The newly confirmed call is still a tested call, and the man who graduates from accountability at ordination has misread the entire process.
Tell the story of your call without embellishment. The temptation to upgrade it into something more dramatic is the old hunger for attention asking for its job back.
Build a path in your church for testing calls: real responsibility, honest evaluation, no shortcuts for the gifted. Do not be hasty in the laying on of hands.
Tell candidates the full cost early, the Mondays as well as the Sundays. A call that needs the brochure version was not ready for testing.

Guard the falsely humble as carefully as the presumptuous. Some of the best shepherds in your congregation are hiding behind unworthiness, and they need the church to come looking, the way the church came for Augustine.
